title: Indian Green Card Wait Hits 179 Years as Per-Country Cap Traps 1.2 Million in Queue
excerpt: A new analysis finds Indian professionals face the longest green card wait times in history, with the EB-2 employment backlog stretching nearly two centuries under the 7% per-country cap.
body:
• Indian professionals applying for EB-2 green cards now face a projected 179-year wait, according to the National Foundation for American Policy
  • The employment-based green card backlog has swelled to 1.2 million people, with Indian nationals making up roughly 79% of applicants
  • Federal law caps each country at 7% of the 140,000 employment-based green cards issued annually, disproportionately penalising applicants from high-demand countries
  • Chinese professionals face an estimated 25-year wait for EB-2 green cards, while applicants from the Philippines wait only months

Indian professionals seeking permanent residency in the United States now face a projected green card wait of 179 years in the most commonly used employment category, a timeline so extreme it effectively amounts to a lifetime ban on legal immigration through that channel.

The figure comes from a new analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), a Virginia-based research group, which found that the employment-based green card backlog has climbed to approximately 1.2 million people. Indian nationals account for about 79% of that queue.

How the 7% Cap Creates a Century-Long Bottleneck

Under current federal immigration law, the United States issues roughly 140,000 employment-based green cards each year. But no single country can receive more than 7% of that allocation, regardless of how many qualified applicants it produces. The result is a system in which workers from countries with large applicant pools — India and China chief among them — are forced into backlogs that stretch decades or longer.

https://x.com/TheGreatAlBundy/status/2095889205133984004

For an Indian professional filing a new labour certification or immigrant petition in January 2026 or later, the NFAP estimates a wait of 179 years in the EB-2 category, the route most commonly used by workers with advanced degrees including master’s holders. The EB-3 category, which covers professionals with bachelor’s degrees and other skilled workers, carries a projected 38-year wait.

Even in the EB-1 category, reserved for individuals with “extraordinary ability” in fields such as science, business, the arts and sports, Indian nationals face a wait of four to five years.

“Many Americans don’t realize how challenging it can be to immigrate legally to the United States, even for the most highly skilled and innovative people in the country. These are people who want to become Americans and are willing to wait years for the chance.”

— Stuart Anderson, Executive Director, National Foundation for American Policy

The Disparity Across Countries

The per-country cap creates stark disparities. A Chinese national applying for an EB-2 green card faces a wait of approximately 25 years — long, but a fraction of the Indian timeline. Workers from the Philippines, by contrast, can expect to wait just months.

The gap reflects the sheer volume of Indian applicants in the system. India’s technology workforce has been the primary feeder of H-1B visa holders for decades, and those workers typically transition to green card applications through their employers. But the per-country cap treats India the same as a country that sends a handful of applicants each year.

Immigration Voice, an advocacy group for skilled immigrants, has described the system as a “de facto Indian Exclusion Act,” arguing that the cap effectively bans any new Indian H-1B holder from ever receiving a green card through the employment-based system.

Impact on Families and Employers

The NFAP warns that the extended wait times make it harder for American employers to recruit and retain foreign-born talent, particularly in technology, healthcare and engineering. Workers stuck in the backlog cannot change jobs freely and face restrictions on travel, tethering them to a single employer for years or decades.

The human cost runs deeper. Spouses on dependent visas face their own work authorisation battles — the Department of Homeland Security recently added a rule to its regulatory agenda that would rescind work permits for H-1B spouses, a move that would compound the hardship. Children of backlogged applicants can “age out” of the system when they turn 21, losing their derivative immigration status entirely and facing potential deportation to a country they may barely know.

What Comes Next

Congressional efforts to eliminate or raise the per-country cap have repeatedly stalled. The EAGLE Act and similar bills have drawn bipartisan support but have never cleared both chambers. Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown has further tightened processing, adding administrative delays to an already paralysed system.

For the estimated one million Indian nationals waiting in line, the arithmetic is unforgiving. At current issuance rates, a professional who enters the EB-2 queue today will not receive a green card in their lifetime — or in the lifetimes of their children and grandchildren.
